content: 1. Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (GTD): GTD encompasses a group of rare tumors that involve abnormal growth of cells inside a woman's uterus. These include hydatidiform moles (complete and partial), invasive moles, choriocarcinoma, placental-site trophoblastic tumors (PSTT), and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors (ETT). Choriocarcinoma, PSTT, and ETT are often grouped under the term gestational trophoblastic tumors. The prognosis for GTD is generally favorable, even in cases where the disease has metastasized to distant organs, particularly if only the lungs are involved. 2. Hydatidiform Mole (HM): A complete mole has a 2% risk of progressing to choriocarcinoma, a malignant form of GTD. Partial moles also carry an increased risk of choriocarcinoma, but the risk is lower compared to complete moles. Women with complete HM are at a higher risk of persistent disease or neoplastic transformation if they exhibit certain characteristics, such as: Age >35 years or <20 years. Pre-evacuation serum beta-hCG levels >100,000 IU/L. A uterus larger than expected for gestational age. Large molar mass or ovarian cysts >6 cm. Complications like preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism, hyperemesis gravidarum, trophoblastic embolization, or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). 3. Follow-Up and Management of GTD: Effective contraception is crucial during the follow-up period to avoid confusion caused by rising beta-hCG levels due to a new pregnancy. Chemotherapy is indicated in cases of: Rising beta-hCG levels over two weeks. Plateauing beta-hCG levels over three weeks. Persistent beta-hCG detection six months after mole evacuation. Tissue diagnosis of choriocarcinoma or the appearance of metastases. Routine work-up for GTD includes: Blood tests for liver, renal, and marrow function. Imaging studies such as chest X-ray, pelvic ultrasound, and, if necessary, head CT or MRI in cases of suspected central nervous system involvement. 4. Treatment of GTD: Treatment depends on the risk category determined by the Modified WHO Prognostic Scoring System, as adapted by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO). Rare forms of GTD, such as PSTT and ETT, are biologically distinct and require separate management strategies. 5. Avian Influenza: For adults, preferred antiviral regimens include oseltamivir (75 mg twice daily for 5 days), zanamivir (10 mg inhaled twice daily for 5 days), or a single intravenous dose of peramivir (600 mg). For children, oseltamivir dosing is weight-based, and zanamivir is an alternative for those who can use inhalation therapy. In cases of severe disease with diarrhea or malabsorption, zanamivir or intravenous peramivir is preferred. Supportive care, including fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, and parenteral nutrition, may be required for critically ill patients. 6. Malaria Treatment: Uncomplicated P. falciparum Malaria: Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are the first-line treatment. Examples include artemether-lumefantrine or artesunate-amodiaquine, with dosing adjusted based on body weight. Severe Malaria: Intravenous or intramuscular artesunate is the preferred treatment for severe malaria in all patient groups, including pregnant women and children. Once the patient stabilizes, oral ACTs are used to complete the treatment course. Special Populations: Pregnant women in the first trimester are treated with quinine and clindamycin, while ACTs are preferred in the second and third trimesters. Infants under 5 kg are treated with ACTs at the same mg/kg dose as older children. Patients co-infected with HIV or tuberculosis require careful selection of antimalarial regimens to avoid drug interactions. 7. Relapse Prevention in P. vivax and P. ovale Malaria: A 14-day course of primaquine is recommended to prevent relapse, except in pregnant women, infants under 6 months, and individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. For G6PD-deficient individuals, weekly primaquine dosing for 8 weeks under close medical supervision is an alternative. 8. Cutaneous Leishmaniasis: Systemic therapy options include sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate, with liposomal amphotericin B as an alternative. Oral miltefosine is another option for adults and adolescents, with dosing based on body weight. Local therapies include cryotherapy, thermotherapy, intralesional antimonials, or topical paromomycin. 9. Babesiosis: Mild to moderate disease is treated with atovaquone and azithromycin for 7–10 days. Severe babesiosis requires clindamycin and quinine, with treatment duration extended in immunocompromised or asplenic patients. 10. Chronic Granulomatous Meningitis: Preferred treatment includes pentamidine combined with clarithromycin or azithromycin, fluconazole, sulfadiazine, and flucytosine.
